title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: Every triangle-free planar graph contains an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $\frac{7}{8}$ of its vertices.
context_text: A graph is $k$-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $k$ (2-degenerate graphs are those whose every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most 2); planar graphs are 5-degenerate and triangle-free planar graphs are 3-degenerate, so the question is how large an induced subgraph of smaller degeneracy one can find. The conjecture would be tight for the cube (the unique 3-regular triangle-free planar graph on 8 vertices), and more generally for every triangle-free planar graph whose vertex set can be partitioned into parts inducing cubes. The authors prove two weaker results: every triangle-free planar graph on $n$ vertices and $m$ edges contains an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $(6n-m-\lambda)/5$ vertices, where $\lambda$ is the number of 'difficult' components, which gives $\frac45 n$ by Euler's formula; and if $G$ has $n_3$ vertices of degree at most three, it contains one on at least $\frac78 n-18n_3$ vertices. This shows that graphs with almost all vertices of degree at least four (which are close to 4-regular grids) are not counterexamples. Analogous problems are the Albertson–Berman conjecture (an induced forest, i.e. an induced 1-degenerate subgraph, on half the vertices of any planar graph) and bounds on induced 3-degenerate subgraphs of planar graphs.
paper_title: Induced 2-degenerate Subgraphs of Triangle-free Planar Graphs

title: Informal belief: 5/6 bound attainable
statement_text: We believe the argument we use can be strengthened to give a bound $\frac{5}{6}$ (every triangle-free planar graph contains an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $\frac{5}{6}$ of its vertices), however the technical issues are substantial and since we do not see this as a viable way to prove in full the conjecture that every triangle-free planar graph contains an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $\frac{7}{8}$ of its vertices, we prefer to present the easier argument giving the bound $\frac{4}{5}$.
context_text: A graph is $k$-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $k$ (2-degenerate graphs are those whose every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most 2); planar graphs are 5-degenerate and triangle-free planar graphs are 3-degenerate, so the question is how large an induced subgraph of smaller degeneracy one can find. The authors prove that every triangle-free planar graph contains an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $\frac45$ of its vertices, via a discharging-type argument giving the bound $(6n-m-\lambda)/5$ for graphs with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges and $\lambda$ components of a special 'difficult' kind (every block a vertex, an edge or a cube, cube blocks vertex-disjoint). The remark is that this method could probably be pushed to $\frac56$, which they do not pursue because it would not reach the conjectured optimal $\frac78$ (tight for the cube). This is an authors' belief about their method rather than a conjecture proper; its mathematical content is that every triangle-free planar graph has an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $\frac56$ of its vertices.
notes: Stated as an authorial belief in running prose, not a labelled environment.
paper_title: Induced 2-degenerate Subgraphs of Triangle-free Planar Graphs
